questions.question: What is a DID (Decentralized Identifier)?
options: A URI in the form did:<method>:<identifier> that resolves to a document the subject controls
A username stored in a central identity registry such as LDAP or Active Directory
A cryptographic hash of the subject's email address
A UUID assigned by the issuing organisation
questions.explanation: A DID is a self-describing URI with three colon-separated parts. It resolves to a DID Document that the subject controls, with no central registry required.

questions.question: In the W3C VC model, which party holds the signed credential?
options: The holder (the subject the credential is about)
The issuer (who created and signed the credential)
The verifier (who checks the credential)
A trusted third-party registry
questions.explanation: After issuance, the holder stores the credential in a wallet. The issuer does not retain a live copy; the holder presents it when needed.

questions.question: Why must the 'proof' field be excluded when computing the proof value over a VC?
options: Including it would create a circular dependency — the proof would cover itself
The proof field is optional and may not exist
JSON-LD processors strip it automatically before signing
HMAC requires the input to be shorter than the key
questions.explanation: You compute the proof over all other fields first, then attach the resulting proof value. Covering the proof field itself is circular and impossible.

questions.question: Why is sort_keys=True essential when serialising a VC for signing?
options: Python dict ordering can vary, and different orderings produce different byte sequences and therefore different HMAC values
JSON-LD requires alphabetical key order by specification
It compresses the JSON payload so HMAC is faster
sort_keys=True is required by the HMAC-SHA256 standard
questions.explanation: Without sort_keys=True the same logical credential can serialise to different byte strings, causing valid credentials to fail verification on a different machine or Python version.

questions.question: What is the main cryptographic weakness of using HMAC-SHA256 as a VC proof in production?
options: HMAC is symmetric — anyone who can verify can also forge, because they hold the same secret key
HMAC-SHA256 is not collision-resistant
HMAC produces a 256-bit output which is too short for VC proofs
HMAC cannot be computed over JSON payloads
questions.explanation: Real VCs use asymmetric signatures (Ed25519, secp256k1) so the issuer's private key signs and anyone with the public key verifies — but cannot forge.

questions.question: What does a Verifiable Presentation (VP) add on top of a VC?
options: A holder-signed envelope that proves the holder chose to share these specific credentials with this verifier
A second issuer signature that re-confirms the claims
An encrypted version of the VC so only the verifier can read it
A timestamp proving when the credential was issued
questions.explanation: The VP proof binds the presentation to the holder's key. Without it, anyone who intercepts the VC could replay it to a different verifier.

questions.question: A holder uses vc_selective_fields to remove the 'age' claim before building a VP. What breaks?
options: The issuer's proof no longer verifies, because the proof was computed over the original full credential subject
Nothing breaks — the issuer's proof only covers the credential metadata, not the claims
The VP holder proof breaks because VPs cannot contain modified VCs
Only the JSON-LD context validation fails; the cryptographic check still passes
questions.explanation: The issuer's HMAC (or real signature) covers the full credentialSubject. Removing a field changes the canonical bytes and invalidates the proof. Production solutions use SD-JWT or BBS+ to avoid this.

questions.question: Which DID method allows a DID to be resolved using standard HTTPS without a blockchain?
options: did:web — the DID Document is hosted at a well-known HTTPS URL on the domain
did:key — the DID Document is derived from the public key with no external lookup
did:ethr — uses Ethereum smart contracts for resolution
did:ion — uses the Bitcoin blockchain as an anchoring layer
questions.explanation: did:web maps a DID to a URL such as https://example.com/.well-known/did.json, making it the easiest method to self-host without blockchain infrastructure.
